title: The Happy Prince
author: Oscar Wilde
tagline: A selfless prince, transformed into a statue, sacrifices all to alleviate the suffering of his city.

characters.name: The Happy Prince
characters.bio: Once a living prince who knew no sorrow, he now stands as a gilded statue overlooking his city. His eyes, now sapphires, shed tears for the widespread misery he beholds. He finds his true purpose in selfless giving.

characters.name: The Swallow
characters.bio: A small bird delayed on his migration to Egypt, he is persuaded by the Happy Prince to stay and assist. He becomes the Prince's devoted companion, delivering precious jewels and gold to the poor. His journey culminates in an ultimate act of loyalty.

characters.name: The Suffering
characters.bio: Representing the various downtrodden individuals in the city, such as the seamstress, the playwright, and the match-girl. Their plights stir the Prince's compassion and motivate his sacrifices. They are the beneficiaries of the Prince's generosity.

characters.name: The Town Officials
characters.bio: A collective of figures like the Mayor and Town Councillors who are more concerned with appearances and regulations than genuine welfare. Their superficiality contrasts sharply with the Prince's true spirit. They ultimately condemn the Prince's altered state.

chapters.title: The Happy Prince
chapters.recap: High above a city, a gilded statue of the Happy Prince looks down upon the widespread poverty and sorrow he never knew in life. A little Swallow, delayed from his migration, takes refuge at the statue's feet and becomes his messenger. Together, they sacrifice the Prince's precious adornments to alleviate human suffering, transforming the city with acts of kindness. Their journey culminates in profound selflessness and a unique form of immortality.

scenes.text:
High above the city, on a tall column, stood the statue of the Happy Prince. He was gilded all over with thin leaves of fine gold, for eyes he had two bright sapphires, and a large red ruby glowed on his sword-hilt.
He was very much admired indeed. 'He is as beautiful as a weathercock,' remarked one of the Town Councillors who wished to gain a reputation for having artistic taste; 'only not quite so useful,' he added, fearing lest people should think him unpractical, which he really was not.
'Why can't you be like the Happy Prince?' asked a sensible mother of her little boy who was crying for the moon. 'The Happy Prince never dreams of crying for anything.'
'I am glad there is some one in the world who is quite happy,' muttered a disappointed man as he gazed at the wonderful statue.
'He looks just like an angel,' said the Charity Children as they came out of the cathedral in their bright scarlet cloaks and their clean white pinafores.
'How do you know?' said the Mathematical Master, 'you have never seen one.'
'Ah! but we have, in our dreams,' answered the Children; and the Mathematical Master frowned and looked very severe, for he did not approve of children dreaming.
One night there flew over the city a little Swallow. His friends had gone away to Egypt six weeks before, but he had stayed behind, for he was in love with the most beautiful Reed. He had met her early in the spring in a bend of the river, and had wooed her with a thousand graceful bows, and had said to her, 'Shall I love you?' but the Reed made no sign.
scenes.label: The Prince's Gaze
scenes.moment: The statue of the Happy Prince stands revered but immobile, unaware of the approaching Swallow who will change his purpose.

scenes.text:
He said to her, 'I will stay with you always,' but the Reed shook her head, she did not like to be married, and a swallow, thought she, is an inconstant creature. She had seen all the dragon-flies that came and went, and she knew that the swallow was prone to wander. He tired of her at last, and said, 'You are a Coquette; I am going to Egypt. Will you come with me?' But the Reed shook her head. 'I have been trifling with you,' he cried, 'and now I shall fly away.' So he flew away, and at last he arrived at the city where the Happy Prince stood. 'Where shall I put myself?' he said. 'I hope the town has made some preparations for me.' Then he saw the statue on the tall column. 'I will put myself there,' he cried; 'it is a fine position with plenty of fresh air.' So he alighted just between the feet of the Happy Prince.
'I have a golden bedroom,' he said softly to himself as he looked round, and he prepared to go to sleep; but just as he was putting his head under his wing a large drop of water fell on him. 'What a curious thing!' he cried. 'There is not a single cloud in the sky, the stars are quite clear and bright, and yet it is raining. The climate of northern Europe is really dreadful. The Reed used to like the rain, but that was mere selfishness on her part.'
Then another drop fell. 'What is the use of a statue if it cannot keep the rain off?' he said; 'I must look for a good chimney-pot.' He determined to fly away; but before he had opened his wings, a third drop fell, and he looked up, and saw—Ah! what did he see?
scenes.label: The Swallow Arrives
scenes.moment: The Swallow, jilted by the Reed, seeks shelter beneath the statue, only to be surprised by falling tears.

scenes.text:
The eyes of the Happy Prince were filled with tears, and tears were running down his golden cheeks. His face was so beautiful in the moonlight that the little Swallow was filled with pity. 'Who are you?' he said. 'I am the Happy Prince.' 'Why are you weeping then?' asked the Swallow; 'you have quite drenched me.' 'When I was alive and had a human heart,' answered the statue, 'I did not know what tears were, for I lived in the Palace of Sans-Souci, where sorrow is not allowed to enter. In the daytime I played with my companions in the garden, and in the evening I led the dance in the Great Hall. Around the garden ran a very lofty wall, but I never cared to ask what lay beyond it. Everything about me was so beautiful. My courtiers called me the Happy Prince, and happy indeed I was, if pleasure be happiness. So I lived, and so I died. And now that I am dead they have set me up here so high that I can see all the ugliness and all the misery of my city, and though my heart is made of lead, yet I cannot choose but weep.'
'What! is he not solid gold?' said the Swallow to himself. He was too polite to make any personal remarks aloud. 'Far away, far away,' continued the Prince in a low musical voice, 'far away in a little street there is a poor house. One of the windows is open, and through it I can see a woman seated at a table. Her face is thin and worn, and she has coarse, red hands, all pricked by the needle, for she is a seamstress. She is embroidering passion-flowers on a satin gown for the loveliest of the Queen's maids-of-honour to wear at the next Court-ball. In a bed in the corner of the room her little boy is lying ill, he has a fever, and is asking for oranges. His mother has nothing to give him but river water, so he is crying. Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow, will you not bring her the ruby out of my sword-hilt? My feet are fastened to this pedestal and I cannot move.'
scenes.label: Prince's Sorrow Revealed
scenes.moment: The statue reveals his leaden heart's sorrow, seeing the city's misery for the first time through his elevated perch.

scenes.text:
'I am waited for in Egypt,' said the Swallow. 'My friends are flying up and down the Nile, and talking to the large lotus-flowers. Soon they will be going to sleep in the tomb of the great King. The King is there himself in his painted coffin. He is wrapped in yellow linen, and embalmed with spices. Round his neck is a chain of pale green jade, and his hands are folded like dead leaves upon his breast.'
'Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,' said the Prince, 'will you not stay with me for one night, and be my messenger? The boy is so thirsty, and the mother so sad.'
The Swallow had a good heart. 'It is very cold here,' he said; 'but I will stay with you for one night, and be your messenger.'
'Thank you, little Swallow,' said the Prince.
So the Swallow picked out the great ruby from the Prince's sword, and flew away with it in his beak over the roofs of the town.
He passed by the cathedral tower, where the white marble angels were sculptured. He passed by the palace and heard the sound of dancing. A beautiful girl came out on the balcony with her lover. 'How wonderful the stars are,' he said to her, 'and how wonderful is the power of love!' 'I hope my dress will be ready in time for the State-ball,' she answered; 'I have ordered passion-flowers to be embroidered on it; but the seamstress are so idle.'
He flew over the river, and saw the lanterns hanging in the masts of the ships. He flew over the Ghetto, and saw the old Jews bargaining with each other, and weighing out money on copper scales. At last he came to the poor house and looked in. The boy was tossing feverishly on his bed, and the mother had fallen asleep, she was so tired. He hopped in, and laid the great ruby on the table beside the woman's thimble. Then he flew gently round the bed, fanning the boy's forehead with his wings. 'How cool I feel!' said the boy, 'I must be getting better'; and he sank into a delicious slumber.
Then the Swallow flew back to the Happy Prince, and told him what he had done. 'It is curious,' he remarked, 'but I feel quite warm now, although it is so cold.'
scenes.label: Ruby to the Seamstress
scenes.moment: The Swallow delivers the ruby, bringing a moment of relief to the feverish boy and a strange warmth to his own heart.

scenes.text:
'That is because you have done a good action,' said the Prince. And the little Swallow began to think, and then he fell asleep. Thinking always made him sleepy.
When day broke he flew down to the river and had a bath. 'To-night I go to Egypt,' said the Swallow, and he was in high spirits at the prospect. He visited all the public monuments, and sat a long time on the top of the church steeple. Wherever he went he heard the sparrows chirping, and saying, 'What a distinguished stranger!' so he enjoyed himself very much.
When evening came he flew back to the Happy Prince. 'Have you any commissions for Egypt?' he cried; 'I am just starting.'
'Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,' said the Prince, 'will you not stay with me one night longer?'
'I am waited for in Egypt,' answered the Swallow. 'To-morrow my friends will fly up to the Second Cataract. The river-horse couches there among the bulrushes, and on a large granite throne sits the God Memnon. All night long he watches the stars, and when the morning star shines he utters one cry of joy, and then he is silent. At noon the yellow lions come down to the water's edge to drink. They have eyes like green beryls, and their roar is louder than the roar of the cataract itself.'
'Far away across the city I see a young man in a garret. He is leaning over a desk covered with papers, and all his hair is brown and crisp, and his lips are red as a pomegranate, and he has large and dreamy eyes. He is trying to finish a play for the Manager of the Theatre, but he is too cold to write any more. There is no fire in the grate, and hunger has made him faint.'
'I will wait with you one night longer,' said the Swallow, who really had a good heart. 'Shall I take him another ruby?'
'Alas! I have no ruby now,' said the Prince; 'my eyes are all that I have left. They are made of rare sapphires, which were brought out of India a thousand years ago. Pluck out one of them, and take it to him. He will sell it to the jeweller, and buy wood and finish his play, and be hungry no longer.'
scenes.label: Sapphire for Playwright
scenes.moment: The Prince, having exhausted his rubies, commands the Swallow to pluck out one of his own sapphire eyes to help a struggling playwright.

scenes.text:
'Dear Prince,' said the Swallow, 'I cannot do that'; and he began to weep. 'Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,' said the Prince, 'do as I command you.' So the Swallow plucked out the Prince's eye, and flew away to the student's garret. It was easy enough to get in, as there was a hole in the roof. Through this he fluttered, and came into the room. The young man had his head buried in his hands, so he did not hear the flutter of the bird's wings, and when he looked up he found the beautiful sapphire lying on the withered violets. 'I am beginning to be appreciated,' he cried; 'this is from some great admirer. Now I can finish my play,' and he looked quite happy.
Next day the Swallow flew down to the harbour. He sat on the mast of a large vessel and watched the sailors hauling big chests out of the hold with ropes. 'Heave ho! heave ho!' they shouted as each chest came up. 'I am going to Egypt!' cried the Swallow, but nobody minded. When the moon rose he flew back to the Happy Prince. 'I am come to bid you good-bye,' he cried. 'Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,' said the Prince, 'will you not stay with me one night longer?' 'It is winter now,' answered the Swallow, 'and the chill snow will soon be here. In Egypt the sun is warm on the green palm-trees, and the crocodiles lie in the mud and look lazily about them. My companions are building a nest in the Temple of Baalbec, and the pink and white doves are watching them, and cooing to each other. Dear Prince, I must leave you, but I will never forget you, and next spring I will bring you back two beautiful jewels in place of those you have given away. The ruby shall be redder than a red rose, and the sapphire shall be as blue as the great ocean.'
scenes.label: Playwright's Sapphire Joy
scenes.moment: The playwright discovers the sapphire, believing it a gift from an admirer, while the Swallow prepares for his final departure.

scenes.text:
'In the square below,' said the Happy Prince, 'there stands a little match-girl. She has let her matches fall in the gutter, and they are all spoiled. Her father will beat her if she does not bring home some money, and she is crying. She has no shoes or stockings, and her little head is bare. Pluck out my other eye, and give it to her, and her father will not beat her.' 'I will stay with you one night longer,' said the Swallow, 'but I cannot pluck out your eye. You would be quite blind then.' 'Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,' said the Prince, 'do as I command you.' So he plucked out the Prince's other eye, and flew down with it. He swooped past the match-girl, and slipped the jewel into the palm of her hand. 'What a lovely bit of glass!' cried the little girl; and she ran home, laughing. Then the Swallow came back to the Prince. 'You are blind now,' he said, 'so I will stay with you always.' 'No, little Swallow,' said the poor Prince, 'you must go away to Egypt.' 'I will stay with you always,' said the Swallow, and he slept at the Prince's feet.
All the next day he sat on the Prince's shoulder, and told him stories of what he had seen in strange lands. He told him of the red ibises who stand in long rows on the banks of the Nile, and catch goldfish in their beaks; of the Sphinx, who is as old as the world itself, and lives in the desert, and knows everything; of the merchants who walk slowly by the side of the camels, and carry amber beads in their hands; of the King of the Mountains of the Moon, who is as black as ebony, and worships a large crystal; and of the great green snake that sleeps upon a palm-tree, and has twenty priests to feed it with honey-cakes.
scenes.label: Last Eye, Loyal Friend
scenes.moment: The Prince sacrifices his last eye for the match-girl, and the Swallow, touched by his complete blindness, pledges to stay forever.

scenes.text:
He told him of the dwarfs who live in the copper mines, and of the giant satyrs who dwell in the great forests and dance the jig with the four winds; of the great white bear who lives in the snow-peaks, and of the reindeer who follow him. But of all he told him, nothing interested the Prince so much as the wonderful things he had seen at home. 'Little Swallow, little Swallow,' said the Prince, 'you are telling me of marvellous things, but more marvellous than anything is the suffering of men and women. There is no Mystery so great as Misery. Fly over my city, little Swallow, and tell me what you see there.' So the Swallow flew over the great city, and saw the rich making merry in their beautiful houses, while the beggars were sitting at the gates. He flew into the dark lanes, and saw the white faces of starving children looking out listlessly at the black streets. Under the archway of a bridge two little boys were lying in one another's arms to try and keep themselves warm. 'How hungry we are!' they said. 'You must not lie here,' shouted a watchman, and they wandered out into the rain. Then he flew back and told the Prince what he had seen. 'I am covered with fine gold,' said the Prince, 'you must take it off, leaf by leaf, and give it to my poor; for the living always think that gold can make them happy.'
Leaf after leaf of the fine gold he picked off, till the Happy Prince looked quite dull and grey. Leaf after leaf he carried to the poor, and the children's faces grew rosier, and they laughed and played in the street. 'We have bread now!' they cried.
scenes.label: Gilding for the Poor
scenes.moment: Witnessing the city's widespread misery, the Prince instructs the Swallow to strip his golden gilding, leaf by leaf, to feed the hungry.

scenes.text:
Then the snow came, and after the snow came the frost. The streets looked as if they were made of silver, they were so bright and glistening; long icicles hung down from the eaves of the houses, everybody went about in furs, and the little birds grew colder and colder.
The poor little Swallow grew colder and colder, but he would not leave the Prince. He loved him too well. He picked up crumbs outside the baker's door when the baker was not looking, and tried to keep himself warm by flapping his wings. But at last he knew that he was going to die. He had just strength enough to fly up to the Prince's shoulder once more. 'Good-bye, dear Prince!' he murmured, 'will you let me kiss your hand?'
'I am glad that you are going to Egypt at last, little Swallow,' said the Prince; 'you have stayed too long here. But you must kiss me on the lips, for I love you.'
'It is not to Egypt that I am going,' said the Swallow. 'I am going to the House of Death. Death is the brother of Sleep, is he not?' And he kissed the Happy Prince on the lips, and fell down dead at his feet.
At that moment a curious crack sound inside the statue. The leaden heart had snapped right in two. It certainly was a dreadfully hard frost.
Early the next morning the Mayor was walking in the promenade below with the Town Councillors. As they passed the column he looked up at the statue: 'Dear me! how shabby the Happy Prince looks!' he said. 'How shabby indeed!' cried the Town Councillors, who always agreed with the Mayor, and they went up to look at it. 'The ruby has fallen out of his sword, his eyes are gone, and he is no longer gilded,' said the Mayor; 'in fact, he looks little better than a beggar! And here is actually a dead bird at his feet!' continued the Mayor. 'We must really issue a proclamation that birds are not to be allowed to die here.' And the Town Clerk made a note of the suggestion. So they pulled down the statue of the Happy Prince. 'As he is no longer beautiful he is no longer useful,' said the Art Professor at the University. Then they melted the statue in a furnace, and the Mayor held a meeting of the Corporation to decide what was to be done with the metal. 'We must have another statue, of course,' he said, 'and it shall be a statue of myself.'
'Of myself,' said each of the Town Councillors, and they quarrelled. When they melted the statue, the overseer of the workmen at the foundry said, 'This broken lead heart will not melt in the furnace. We must throw it away.' So they threw it on a dust-heap where the dead Swallow was also lying.
'Bring me the two most precious things in the city,' said God to one of His Angels; and the Angel brought Him the leaden heart and the dead bird. 'You have rightly chosen,' said God, 'for in my garden of Paradise this little bird shall sing for evermore, and in my city of gold the Happy Prince shall praise me.'
scenes.label: Sacrifice and Immortality
scenes.moment: The Swallow dies of cold at the Prince's feet, his leaden heart snaps, and both are taken to God as the city officials dismiss their sacrifices.

gilded.definition: Covered thinly with gold leaf or gold paint.

weathercock.definition: A weather vane, typically in the shape of a rooster.

pinafores.definition: Sleeveless garments worn as aprons or dresses.

reed.definition: A tall, slender-leaved plant of the grass family that grows in water or marshy ground.

wooed.definition: Tried to gain the love or affection of someone.

alighted.definition: Descended from the air and settled.

courtiers.definition: People who attend a royal court as companions or advisers to the monarch.

pedestal.definition: The base or support on which a statue, obelisk, or column is mounted.

seamstress.definition: A woman who sews, especially one who earns her living by sewing.

embroidering.definition: Decorating cloth by sewing patterns on it with thread.

passion-flowers.definition: Tropical climbing plants with elaborate flowers.

satin gown.definition: A dress made of a smooth, glossy fabric.

thimble.definition: A small metal or plastic cap worn on the finger to protect it when sewing.

bulrushes.definition: Tall, stout, grasslike plants growing in wet places.

granite throne.definition: A seat of power made from a hard, igneous rock.

memnon.definition: A mythical king of Ethiopia, often associated with a colossal statue in Egypt.

beryils.definition: Transparent gemstones, typically green, blue, or yellow.

garret.definition: A top-floor or attic room, often small and cramped.

pomegranate.definition: A round, reddish fruit containing many seeds in a juicy, edible pulp.

grate.definition: A framework of bars, typically in a fireplace.

ghetto.definition: A part of a city, especially a slum area, occupied by a minority group.

amber beads.definition: Small, polished pieces of solidified tree resin, used as jewellery.

satyrs.definition: Mythological creatures, half-man and half-goat, known for revelry.

ibises.definition: Wading birds with long, downcurved bills.

sphinx.definition: A mythical creature with the head of a human and the body of a lion.

archway.definition: A curved structure forming a passageway or a support.

watchman.definition: A person employed to look after an empty building or property.

eaves.definition: The part of a roof that meets or overhangs the walls of a building.

shabby.definition: In poor condition through long or hard use or lack of care; scruffy.

proclamation.definition: A public or official announcement, especially one dealing with a matter of great importance.

corporation.definition: A municipal body charged with the government of a town or city.

foundry.definition: A factory where metal castings are produced.

dust-heap.definition: A pile of refuse or rubbish.
